Many individuals exploring new opportunities choose to work with recruiters, but doing so can sometimes limit your options. When a recruiter submits your resume to a firm on your behalf, the firm is typically required to pay a placement fee if you are hired. In many cases, that fee can be 20% or more of the starting salary. Because of this, some firms may choose not to pursue a candidate they otherwise might have considered if there were no associated recruiting fee. If there is a firm you are particularly interested in, consider reaching out to them directly. Sending a well-written, professional resume along with a thoughtful cover letter can significantly improve your chances of securing an initial conversation.

I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

Posting and praying is not recruiting. A WORD TO RECRUITERS AND THEIR JOB PLACEMENT AGENCIES Almost every month I see new ads on LinkedIn (and other sites) for new agencies offering job assistance. And every one of them wants members to pay a monthly fee for services that may or may not land them any jobs. There are hundreds of services like yours. What makes yours the right choice? Job seekers don’t need another subscription service to pay monthly. They need recruiters who understand how to match real talent with real hiring needs — not firms that scan resumes for keywords and push them through applicant systems for hundreds of dollars per month. That isn’t recruiting. That's automation. Real placement means understanding a candidate’s strengths and building relationships with companies that actually need the talent. In legitimate recruiting, the employer -- not the job seeker -- pays the fee. Employers either pay a placement fee or a percentage markup (often 10–20%) on a contractor’s hourly rate for a set period of time. Many professionals are no longer willing to pay $300–$500+ per month for vague promises with no guaranteed outcome. With scams increasing on LinkedIn and elsewhere, skepticism is common sense. What’s more, most experienced professionals don’t need resume rewrites or generic coaching. They need access to real hiring managers and real opportunities. If your firm truly operates differently, explain: • Who pays your fee? • How do you engage employers? • What measurable results do you deliver? Transparency builds trust. Anything else raises concerns.

I always wonder how much a SAP recruiting agency charges for a consultant on a contract type of project. Today I've asked ChatGPT : 😁 Because SAP professionals often possess highly specialized skills, agencies frequently command the higher end of this range (20–30%) for roles such as S/4HANA consultants, architects, or niche module experts. Key Aspects of SAP Recruitment Fees: Contractor Markups (Temp): For contract positions, agencies typically charge a markup on the hourly or daily rate, which can range from 25% to 75% 🤯 above the contractor's pay, or 15–30% of the annualised salary. Guarantee Period: Contracts usually include a 30- to 90-day guarantee period, during which the agency must replace the candidate for free if they leave. Factors Influencing Fee Percentages: Scarcity: Highly specialized SAP modules (e.g., EWM, IBP, BTP) command higher fees due to limited talent pools. Exclusivity: If a company gives an agency exclusive rights to fill a role, they might negotiate a lower percentage, but for competitive "headhunting" scenarios, fees are higher. Location: Rates vary by region, with higher salary markets often driving higher absolute fee amounts. Common Fee Structures: Percentage of Salary: Standard 15-30% of the first-year compensation (base + bonus). Retained Search: Used for senior SAP leadership, involving an upfront fee (often 1/3 of total) and 25-35% total commission. Flat Fee: A set price regardless of salary, sometimes used for high-volume, lower-level roles. What do you think, are these values real, or have you heard of even worse cases? What do you think is a decent fee? P.S. I was in a project were I got 30% of the total what the customer payed.

I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

What is the downside of giving a state agency the authority to investigate and resolve those complaints? There is an obvious cost to run the state agency. Spread across millions of taxpayers, it is a relatively small cost per citizen. But many people don’t live in associations, and they have to subsidize the cost of resolving someone’s else’s grievance that has no impact on their life. But the question is more interesting when we look at the cost of running a state agency on a per-dispute basis. How much does it cost to resolve each dispute? According to the internet (so the data could be rough), our state received about 800 HOA complaints in 2018, when manager licensing was in effect. About 220 of those were manager licensing complaints. Some of these 800 complaints were duplicative, meaning that the same person filed the same complaint more than once. This is for a state that has about 2.5 million people living in HOAs. Also according to the internet, the office of HOA licensing operated on a budget of about $700,000 for 2018. So the cost to run the agency on a per-complaint basis in 2018 was about $3,200. That doesn't factor in the time of managers to respond to the complaints. I do know that in responding to some of the complaints, the time was significant. Others were disposed of without needing a response. Not all complaints are the same. Some involved serious violations that resulted in revocation of a license. Others were frivolous. The policy question in my mind is whether a complaining owner should pay a deposit or a fee for making a complaint with the state agency?

Sharing an observation that keeps confirming itself in real projects. I’m not claiming absolute truth, but there are clear signs that the traditional digital agency model may change significantly in the next few years. I’m talking about agencies whose business is built around a percentage of ad spend. This model has worked for the last 10–15 years, but today it’s becoming less stable. First, in-house teams are no longer expensive. The labor market has changed, and more companies prefer to build marketing internally. It gives better control, deeper product understanding, and direct connection to business KPIs (assuming KPIs are aligned across departments — which is another story). Second, technology is rapidly reducing the value of manual work. Campaign setup, optimization, and analytics are increasingly automated. The role of humans in classic media buying is gradually shrinking. Third, advertising platforms themselves are reducing the need for intermediaries. We see this across all global platforms: — stricter partner requirements — lower bonuses — smaller commissions, often moving toward zero The logic is simple: the more automation, the less the platform needs an agency. Fourth, agency economics are becoming fragile. Clients are used to paying a small percentage — sometimes 1–2% of the budget — and competition keeps margins low. In many cases, the model survives only because of platform commissions. Once those disappear, a large number of agencies will lose profitability. So the real question is not whether the market will change, but whether agencies will adapt in time. In my view, the window for strategic decisions is about one year. After that, the room for maneuver will shrink quickly. In two years, it may be gone. If you run an agency business, this might be the right moment to rethink the model. There are transformation scenarios available, but the time to think is getting shorter. Feel free to reach me out — let’s discuss. Every situation is different, but solutions still exist. Companies are just as confused about creating RFPs as they are about creating the software itself. And it makes complete sense when you think about it. The company is outsourcing a solution because they're not capable of building it themselves. That's great. But they're also the wrong people to write the RFP. Here's what actually happens: one person thinks of the solution they want, or three people try to write it simultaneously, or someone throws it through ChatGPT. The result is an RFP that prescribes solutions instead of describing problems. Then consulting agencies read that RFP and their goal is to win the contract. So they say yes to as much as possible, even if it doesn't make sense. They think they'll clear it up later during the SOW phase. But then what happens? The biz dev person at the agency and the main contact at the company want to get the contract done as fast as possible. The company wants to hit deadlines. The agency wants signatures so money can flow. Usually the biz dev people aren't the ones doing technical or design work. They're often paid on commission, which means they're super oriented to getting signatures. So if you try to slow down the SOW process to get clarity, it's not often successful. You launch a contract where the RFP was confusing, the SOW reflects that confusion, and now everybody expects the wrong things. The real solution? Companies should pay professionals to do a discovery process and write the RFP. Most startups get their first people hire completely wrong. Not because they hire badly. Because they hire too late - and then too fast. The founding team holds everything together through sheer willpower until about 30 people. Then the cracks appear. Hiring slows down. Offers start to get rejected. Two senior people leave within the same quarter. So they panic and hire a Head of HR. But the problem was never HR. The problem was that nobody ever defined what good looked like for this specific business, at this specific stage, with this specific culture. An HR hire without that foundation doesn't fix the problem. They just inherit it. The companies that scale their people function without breaking do something different. They answer three questions before they make a single people hire: 💡 What does the business need from its people in the next 18 months - not today? 💡 What does our culture actually look like right now, versus what we say it looks like? 💡 What people infrastructure needs to exist before we can hire someone to run it? The answers are uncomfortable because they likely delay the immediate decisions you crave. But they're the difference between a people function that enables growth and one that slows it down.

Should you hire Sales or Marketing first? I’ve discussed with founders at early-stage startups and it’s something you really don’t want to get wrong. Startups have limited runway, and making the wrong hires can see you burn through that without the results you’d hoped for. If you hire sales too early, you have an expensive AE with no real pipeline, no clear ICP, and no repeatable message. If you hire marketing too early, you generate interest without a defined sales motion to convert it. Once prospects turn away disappointed, it will be very difficult to win them back. The truth is, there isn’t a universal answer. It depends on your product, your pricing, and what the founder can already do themselves. In general though: Hire Sales first if: - You’re selling high-ticket, complex deals that require discovery and negotiation. - The founder is closing deals but running out of time. - You already have inbound or warm intros, but conversion is the bottleneck. Hire Marketing first if: - Your model relies on volume, lower annual contract value, or product-led growth. - The founders can sell, but nobody knows who you are yet. - You’re creating a new category and you need to create demand before outbound works. My advice to founders is to wait before hiring either role until you’ve personally closed your first 10 customers who didn’t already know you. Get it working yourself first. Then hire to scale it.

Here's a frequent tension we see in the best / fastest growing Hard Tech startups: Demand for product is real. Customers want it yesterday. Need is urgent. BD team / leadership want to deliver on it and vacuum up all the demand today. This is the core of what drives fundraising momentum, especially at growth stages. But engineering needs to actually build the product(s)! And they're short resources. Hiring is hard. BD pushes forward anyway. "We won the contract!" Head of Engineering says "but how do we resource it / prioritize?" Engineering gets mad at BD for going too fast. BD gets mad at engineering for being negative. CEO is caught in the middle needing to pick a side. Investors want more revenue. Customers want things on time. Engineering wants to deliver great work ahead of schedule. This is hard! Do you compromise on eng talent quality and hire faster to meet contract deadlines? Do you say no to new contracts you'd easily win to make sure you deliver on contracts you already have? What's the solve? It's not an easy one! Solve 1: give your leaders more agency than it might seem their experience warrants. If they have good judgement, they'll figure it out. Solve 2: give these leaders cash to solve the problem...if you can raise it. Solve 3: delay deliverables if you have to. You're likely already 2x faster than a legacy player anyway. But be transparent with the customer as things develop. It builds trust. Saying "no" to real contracts now feels safe, but may be long term damaging. It's hard to mobilize customer interest, need to strike while the iron's hot and resource aggressively in other ways. Anyone have different views on this?

Jeremy Gnozzo at Search Solution Group said something this week that caught my attention: in 2026, precision will matter more than speed in hiring. And he’s right. Most leaders think they’re being precise when they write detailed job descriptions. But that’s not where the real work happens. Real precision means answering the hard questions before you post the role: -- What’s the actual pace of work? Are we talking startup speed or enterprise methodical? -- Where does decision-making authority really sit? What can this person own vs. what needs approval? -- What does success look like in 90 days? In six months? Be specific. -- What are the unwritten rules of how work gets done here? Here’s the thing; we’ve all seen it. A company rushes to fill a seat, then six months later everyone’s frustrated. What do we blame? We blame the speed of the hire. But speed isn’t the problem. Moving fast is fine when you know exactly what you’re looking for. The problem is ambiguity. Vague expectations. Undefined success metrics. Unclear authority. That’s what creates mismatched hires, not the clock. I've seen this everywhere from offices to film sets. So before your next hire, pause... Get brutally specific about what this role actually needs to deliver and how they’ll work within your system. The job description is the easy part. The real work is defining the role with enough precision that both you and your new hire know exactly what winning looks like. What’s one question you wish you’d answered before your last hire?

This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

You're not bad at making hard calls, you're just making them at the wrong time of day. In his latest piece, Phil McKinney challenges the old myth that decision-making “drains” like a battery. The research doesn’t support that story. What studies found instead is that after long periods of mental effort, your brain starts to change how it works. It leans toward what is faster and easier instead of what is deeper and more accurate. Careful thinking begins to feel like too much work, and your standards slowly drop without you realizing it. That is decision fatigue, and it usually shows up in small ways: - Nodding to a plan you would’ve challenged in the morning - Snapping at reasonable questions - Making a 30-minute decision in 30 seconds - Feeling relieved when someone else decides for you McKinney’s most practical advice is to stop relying on discipline in the moment and start building guardrails in advance. Pre-commitments such as setting rules about budget approvals late in the day, delaying responses to emotionally charged emails, or avoiding major hiring decisions at the end of the week create protection. They allow your high-energy self to safeguard your low-energy self. I featured Phil McKinney's insights in this week's issue of Exec Engineering. Reverse Recruiting in the UK! Is It even LEGAL? I’ve just read a recent piece discussing the rise of reverse recruitment. Where “career agents” charge candidates monthly fees and up to 10% of their salary to secure a role. This trend is growing fast in the US, and now appears to be creeping into the UK. But there’s a major problem:In the UK, it is illegal for recruiters to charge candidates to find them work. This isn’t a grey area. It’s clearly set out in UK law: The Employment Agencies Act 1973 prohibits agencies from charging individuals for finding them work (except in a few narrowly defined cases such as modelling and entertainment). The Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 reinforce this and regulate agency behaviour. GOV.UK also states plainly: “Recruitment agencies cannot charge you a fee for finding or trying to find you work.” Agencies can charge for optional services such as CV writing, training, or career coaching BUT they cannot make these a condition of finding you work. Some of these companies operate from the US or market themselves as “career agents,” not recruiters, positioning their fees as payment for coaching or networking support rather than job placement. But if a UK‑based business takes money in exchange for trying to secure you a job, it crosses a legal boundary. With unemployment rising and the job market tightening, the risk is that desperate candidates get exploited under the banner of “premium job‑search support.” My view UK jobseekers need to be very cautious. If you are paying anyone who claims to help you secure a role in the UK, ask direct questions: Are you compliant with UK recruitment legislation? Are you charging for coaching, or for job placement? Are your services optional or tied to finding me employment? Do you operate legally within the UK? If the answers get vague: Walk away! https://lnkd.in/ew-5kPzv

Everyone Wants “Top Talent,” but Few Can Define It. In tech and product teams, the phrase “top talent” gets thrown around constantly. But when you dig into it, most companies can’t actually articulate what that means for their environment. They’ll say things like: “We want someone strategic.” “We need a builder.” “We want someone who can scale.” “We need a product leader who’s technical but not too technical.” None of that is wrong — it’s just not specific enough to hire against. Because in tech, “top talent” is entirely contextual. A great PM in a 20‑person startup is not the same as a great PM in a 2,000‑person org. A strong engineering leader in a high‑ambiguity environment may fail in a process‑heavy one. A “builder” in one company is a “disruptor” in another — and not always in a good way. The real work in tech hiring isn’t finding impressive résumés. It’s defining the environment the person is walking into: - How much ambiguity exists? - How fast are decisions made? - What’s the engineering culture really like? - How much political navigation is required? - What does “success” look like in the first 90 days? - What’s broken that no one wants to say out loud? When companies skip this step, they don’t hire “top talent.” They hire someone who looks great on paper and hope it works out. When they get it right, the difference is immediate — alignment, velocity, clarity, and fewer surprises on both sides. Tech hiring isn’t about finding the best person. It’s about finding the best person for this exact environment, at this exact moment. That’s where the real precision lives. Startup Finance Insight #2 – The Fixed Cost Trap A founder raised ₹2 Cr by diluting ~33% equity. But the funding was structured differently. Instead of receiving the entire amount upfront, the funds were to be released monthly, with shares transferring accordingly. Midway through the funding cycle, the investor’s management changed. The new team told the founder: “Show revenue traction first, then we will release the remaining funds.” Suddenly the startup had to rethink its strategy with limited capital. The founder shared a revised plan: • Hire a full social media team • Spend ₹3 Lakhs per month on ads At first glance, it looked like an aggressive growth push. But the bigger risk was cost rigidity. Hiring employees converts uncertainty into fixed monthly burn. Instead, suggested focusing on B2B revenue to build investor confidence, and using external agencies instead of hiring full-time employees. Why? Because agencies provide flexibility. If campaigns don’t work or the product needs to pivot, the startup can pause or change direction quickly. Employees, on the other hand, immediately become fixed costs. And early-stage startups rarely fail because of bad ideas. They fail because costs become fixed before revenue becomes predictable. Financial discipline at early stages is often about preserving flexibility. #StartupFinance #Founders #VirtualCFO #StartupLessons #BurnRate #Startups

Counting the Cost Having a great idea is a strong starting point — but it’s only the beginning of building a successful business. Many people have hobbies or interests that can be transformed into profitable ventures. However, passion and a strong product or service alone will not sustain a business. Strong businesses are built on solid financial foundations, and if you want to run a profitable business, you must understand your costs. Knowing your true costs allows you to set prices that not only cover your expenses but also generate the income you deserve. Without that clarity, you risk underpricing, overworking, and limiting your growth. Calculating your costs may feel overwhelming at first — but it’s more straightforward than you think. You just need a clear, disciplined approach. At its core, calculating costs come down to three key components: 1. Materials – What it takes to produce your product or deliver your service. 2. Labor – The time and effort required (including your own) 3. Overhead – The operating expenses that must be allocated to each unit. When you consistently account for these elements, you move from guessing to leading with strategy. Start with your materials. Identify every ingredient or component that goes into your product. Determine how much of each item is required to produce one unit, then break down the total purchase cost to figure out the cost per unit. Once you have done that for each component, add them together to determine your total material cost. Next, factor in labor. Be honest about the value of your time. If someone hired you to produce this product or deliver this service, what would you charge? Assign that amount to each unit. Your time is not free — and your pricing should reflect that. Then, account for overhead. These are your ongoing business expenses — rent, utilities, software, equipment, insurance, and more. Allocate a reasonable portion of those total costs to each unit you produce or service you deliver. Whether manufacturing products or providing services — the process will be manageable once you break it down step by step. And here’s the key: once you establish your cost structure, you can apply it consistently to similar products or services. That clarity allows you to price confidently, protect your margins, and lead your business with intention.

Commission + W-2: The Structural Conflict Insurance Rarely Examines We talk about ethics in insurance. We rarely talk about incentive architecture. Most independent agencies operate under: • W-2 employment • Commission-based revenue • Growth quotas • Carrier incentives • Revenue-based valuation metrics It works operationally. But structurally, it creates tension and that tension surfaces in litigation. Retention vs. Growth New business drives: • Higher commission • Bonuses • Carrier incentives • Agency valuation Remarketing a renewal to reduce premium may: • Reduce revenue • Reduce compensation • Reduce valuation multiples So when time is finite, where does it go? A producer can deeply review renewals… Or write new accounts that move production metrics. The system answers that question before the employee consciously does. This isn’t about bad actors. It’s about incentives shaping behavior. Why Attorneys Should Care Compensation design is discoverable. In coverage disputes or broker liability cases, counsel asks: • What was the renewal review protocol? • Were alternative markets evaluated? • Was remarketing considered? • How were producers compensated? If growth is rewarded more visibly than optimization, that matters. Not because commission is improper. But because incentives influence conduct. And conduct leaves patterns. E&O Risk Is Often Structural When growth pressure dominates: • Renewals become transactional • Market evaluations are inconsistent • Internal rewrites that reduce premium are deprioritized • Coverage gaps persist across renewals Even defensible cases become expensive when documentation is thin. The Internal Rewrite Problem If an internal rewrite lowers premium, and lowers commission, what incentive exists to prioritize it? If none exists, that becomes uncomfortable in deposition. This is not moral judgment. It’s structural exposure. Structural Reform If agencies want stronger defensibility: • Tie compensation to documented renewal review • Reward retention quality, not just growth • Separate advisory compensation where appropriate • Formalize market evaluation protocols This is risk mitigation, not theory. Insurance is one of the only industries where doing right by the client can reduce revenue. Layer that onto W-2 employment and growth metrics, and tension becomes systemic. The industry doesn’t have an ethics crisis. It has an incentive alignment crisis. And incentive alignment drives liability. Shelby King Hayes, CIC, CPRM Insurance Consultant | Coverage Strategy | Expert Witness

Jeremy Gnozzo at Search Solution Group said something this week that caught my attention: in 2026, precision will matter more than speed in hiring. And he’s right. Most leaders think they’re being precise when they write detailed job descriptions. But that’s not where the real work happens. Real precision means answering the hard questions before you post the role: -- What’s the actual pace of work? Are we talking startup speed or enterprise methodical? -- Where does decision-making authority really sit? What can this person own vs. what needs approval? -- What does success look like in 90 days? In six months? Be specific. -- What are the unwritten rules of how work gets done here? Here’s the thing; we’ve all seen it. A company rushes to fill a seat, then six months later everyone’s frustrated. What do we blame? We blame the speed of the hire. But speed isn’t the problem. Moving fast is fine when you know exactly what you’re looking for. The problem is ambiguity. Vague expectations. Undefined success metrics. Unclear authority. That’s what creates mismatched hires, not the clock. I've seen this everywhere from offices to film sets. So before your next hire, pause... Get brutally specific about what this role actually needs to deliver and how they’ll work within your system. The job description is the easy part. The real work is defining the role with enough precision that both you and your new hire know exactly what winning looks like. What’s one question you wish you’d answered before your last hire?

Hiring someone because you are overwhelmed and need a body in a seat is how you create a bigger problem six months from now. Here's a frequent tension we see in the best / fastest growing Hard Tech startups: Demand for product is real. Customers want it yesterday. Need is urgent. BD team / leadership want to deliver on it and vacuum up all the demand today. This is the core of what drives fundraising momentum, especially at growth stages. But engineering needs to actually build the product(s)! And they're short resources. Hiring is hard. BD pushes forward anyway. "We won the contract!" Head of Engineering says "but how do we resource it / prioritize?" Engineering gets mad at BD for going too fast. BD gets mad at engineering for being negative. CEO is caught in the middle needing to pick a side. Investors want more revenue. Customers want things on time. Engineering wants to deliver great work ahead of schedule. This is hard! Do you compromise on eng talent quality and hire faster to meet contract deadlines? Do you say no to new contracts you'd easily win to make sure you deliver on contracts you already have? What's the solve? It's not an easy one! Solve 1: give your leaders more agency than it might seem their experience warrants. If they have good judgement, they'll figure it out. Solve 2: give these leaders cash to solve the problem...if you can raise it. Solve 3: delay deliverables if you have to. You're likely already 2x faster than a legacy player anyway. But be transparent with the customer as things develop. It builds trust. Saying "no" to real contracts now feels safe, but may be long term damaging. It's hard to mobilize customer interest, need to strike while the iron's hot and resource aggressively in other ways. Anyone have different views on this?

Should you hire Sales or Marketing first? I’ve discussed with founders at early-stage startups and it’s something you really don’t want to get wrong. Startups have limited runway, and making the wrong hires can see you burn through that without the results you’d hoped for. If you hire sales too early, you have an expensive AE with no real pipeline, no clear ICP, and no repeatable message. If you hire marketing too early, you generate interest without a defined sales motion to convert it. Once prospects turn away disappointed, it will be very difficult to win them back. The truth is, there isn’t a universal answer. It depends on your product, your pricing, and what the founder can already do themselves. In general though: Hire Sales first if: - You’re selling high-ticket, complex deals that require discovery and negotiation. - The founder is closing deals but running out of time. - You already have inbound or warm intros, but conversion is the bottleneck. Hire Marketing first if: - Your model relies on volume, lower annual contract value, or product-led growth. - The founders can sell, but nobody knows who you are yet. - You’re creating a new category and you need to create demand before outbound works. My advice to founders is to wait before hiring either role until you’ve personally closed your first 10 customers who didn’t already know you. Get it working yourself first. Then hire to scale it.

I’m not claiming absolute truth, but there are clear signs that the traditional digital agency model may change significantly in the next few years. I’m talking about agencies whose business is built around a percentage of ad spend. This model has worked for the last 10–15 years, but today it’s becoming less stable. First, in-house teams are no longer expensive. The labor market has changed, and more companies prefer to build marketing internally. It gives better control, deeper product understanding, and direct connection to business KPIs (assuming KPIs are aligned across departments — which is another story). Second, technology is rapidly reducing the value of manual work. Campaign setup, optimization, and analytics are increasingly automated. The role of humans in classic media buying is gradually shrinking. Third, advertising platforms themselves are reducing the need for intermediaries. We see this across all global platforms: — stricter partner requirements — lower bonuses — smaller commissions, often moving toward zero The logic is simple: the more automation, the less the platform needs an agency. Fourth, agency economics are becoming fragile. Clients are used to paying a small percentage — sometimes 1–2% of the budget — and competition keeps margins low. In many cases, the model survives only because of platform commissions. Once those disappear, a large number of agencies will lose profitability. So the real question is not whether the market will change, but whether agencies will adapt in time. In my view, the window for strategic decisions is about one year. After that, the room for maneuver will shrink quickly. In two years, it may be gone. If you run an agency business, this might be the right moment to rethink the model. Companies are just as confused about creating RFPs as they are about creating the software itself. And it makes complete sense when you think about it. The company is outsourcing a solution because they're not capable of building it themselves. That's great. But they're also the wrong people to write the RFP. Here's what actually happens: one person thinks of the solution they want, or three people try to write it simultaneously, or someone throws it through ChatGPT. The result is an RFP that prescribes solutions instead of describing problems. Then consulting agencies read that RFP and their goal is to win the contract. So they say yes to as much as possible, even if it doesn't make sense. They think they'll clear it up later during the SOW phase. But then what happens? The biz dev person at the agency and the main contact at the company want to get the contract done as fast as possible. The company wants to hit deadlines. The agency wants signatures so money can flow. Usually the biz dev people aren't the ones doing technical or design work. They're often paid on commission, which means they're super oriented to getting signatures. So if you try to slow down the SOW process to get clarity, it's not often successful. You launch a contract where the RFP was confusing, the SOW reflects that confusion, and now everybody expects the wrong things. The real solution? Companies should pay professionals to do a discovery process and write the RFP. People who understand technology, process, and design can write an RFP that enables agencies to show how they'll solve problems, not deliver to solutions that don't make sense. It's not even that expensive. But we've gotten away from this in tech. #ConsultingTruth #RFPProcess #DiscoveryMatters

This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

You're not bad at making hard calls, you're just making them at the wrong time of day. In his latest piece, Phil McKinney challenges the old myth that decision-making “drains” like a battery. It leans toward what is faster and easier instead of what is deeper and more accurate. Careful thinking begins to feel like too much work, and your standards slowly drop without you realizing it. That is decision fatigue, and it usually shows up in small ways: - Nodding to a plan you would’ve challenged in the morning - Snapping at reasonable questions - Making a 30-minute decision in 30 seconds - Feeling relieved when someone else decides for you McKinney’s most practical advice is to stop relying on discipline in the moment and start building guardrails in advance. Pre-commitments such as setting rules about budget approvals late in the day, delaying responses to emotionally charged emails, or avoiding major hiring decisions at the end of the week create protection. Key Aspects of SAP Recruitment Fees: Contractor Markups (Temp): For contract positions, agencies typically charge a markup on the hourly or daily rate, which can range from 25% to 75% 🤯 above the contractor's pay, or 15–30% of the annualised salary. Guarantee Period: Contracts usually include a 30- to 90-day guarantee period, during which the agency must replace the candidate for free if they leave. Factors Influencing Fee Percentages: Scarcity: Highly specialized SAP modules (e.g., EWM, IBP, BTP) command higher fees due to limited talent pools. Exclusivity: If a company gives an agency exclusive rights to fill a role, they might negotiate a lower percentage, but for competitive "headhunting" scenarios, fees are higher. Location: Rates vary by region, with higher salary markets often driving higher absolute fee amounts. I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

Reverse Recruiting in the UK! Is It even LEGAL? I’ve just read a recent piece discussing the rise of reverse recruitment. Where “career agents” charge candidates monthly fees and up to 10% of their salary to secure a role. This trend is growing fast in the US, and now appears to be creeping into the UK. But there’s a major problem:In the UK, it is illegal for recruiters to charge candidates to find them work. This isn’t a grey area. It’s clearly set out in UK law: The Employment Agencies Act 1973 prohibits agencies from charging individuals for finding them work (except in a few narrowly defined cases such as modelling and entertainment). The Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 reinforce this and regulate agency behaviour. GOV.UK also states plainly: “Recruitment agencies cannot charge you a fee for finding or trying to find you work.” Agencies can charge for optional services such as CV writing, training, or career coaching BUT they cannot make these a condition of finding you work. Some of these companies operate from the US or market themselves as “career agents,” not recruiters, positioning their fees as payment for coaching or networking support rather than job placement. But if a UK‑based business takes money in exchange for trying to secure you a job, it crosses a legal boundary. With unemployment rising and the job market tightening, the risk is that desperate candidates get exploited under the banner of “premium job‑search support.” My view UK jobseekers need to be very cautious. If you are paying anyone who claims to help you secure a role in the UK, ask direct questions: Are you compliant with UK recruitment legislation? Are you charging for coaching, or for job placement? Engineers should be careful about where their resume ends up. They know their bosses know other bosses. They know information travels. Once a resume is out, it’s out. A lot of recruiting companies don’t respect that. I've seen recruiters lift jobs from LinkedIn, reword them slightly (terribly redone with AI) and post them as their own without even having an agreement with the company. They’re hoping to get a candidate first so they can force the relationship with your resume. That approach burns trust on both sides. The way I handle it is slower and confidential on the front end, but cleaner. If an engineer reaches out and we don’t already have the perfect role, I blind their resume. I take all identifying information off. I summarize their background. Then I go to companies on their behalf and say, “Here’s a 10 year geotechnical engineer. PE. Foundation design. Materials. This is the kind of work they’ve been doing. Would you have a need for someone like this?” If the answer is yes, then we get an agreement in place. Only after that do I go back to the engineer and say, “This company wants to talk. Are you okay with me sharing your resume?” That protects everyone. No surprises. No information floating around without permission. Engineers notice and seem to appreciate that difference.

Not because they lack skill. Not because their experience is weak. But because alignment is missing. Here are the most common reasons qualified engineers don’t move forward. • The experience is adjacent, not direct. Hiring managers often need someone who has solved a very specific problem before. If your experience is similar but not clearly connected, the signal gets lost. • The resume hides the important work. Dense paragraphs and long tool lists bury the parts that actually matter. If the reader has to hunt for your value, momentum disappears. • The story isn’t clear. Hiring teams want to understand what you owned, what you decided, and what changed because of your work. When ownership is vague, confidence drops. • Communication creates uncertainty. In interviews, clarity matters as much as correctness. If your thinking is hard to follow, hiring managers struggle to picture you on the team. Here’s the important shift. Most rejections are not judgments about ability. They are decisions about fit for a very specific role at a specific moment. Qualified engineers don’t lose because they aren’t capable. They lose because another job seeker made the alignment easier to see, or their experience was more aligned. Make the signal obvious. Show the problem you solved. Explain the decision you made. Highlight the impact you created. I always wonder how much a SAP recruiting agency charges for a consultant on a contract type of project. Today I've asked ChatGPT : 😁 Because SAP professionals often possess highly specialized skills, agencies frequently command the higher end of this range (20–30%) for roles such as S/4HANA consultants, architects, or niche module experts. Key Aspects of SAP Recruitment Fees: Contractor Markups (Temp): For contract positions, agencies typically charge a markup on the hourly or daily rate, which can range from 25% to 75% 🤯 above the contractor's pay, or 15–30% of the annualised salary. Guarantee Period: Contracts usually include a 30- to 90-day guarantee period, during which the agency must replace the candidate for free if they leave. Factors Influencing Fee Percentages: Scarcity: Highly specialized SAP modules (e.g., EWM, IBP, BTP) command higher fees due to limited talent pools. Exclusivity: If a company gives an agency exclusive rights to fill a role, they might negotiate a lower percentage, but for competitive "headhunting" scenarios, fees are higher. Location: Rates vary by region, with higher salary markets often driving higher absolute fee amounts. I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

Should you hire Sales or Marketing first? I’ve discussed with founders at early-stage startups and it’s something you really don’t want to get wrong. Startups have limited runway, and making the wrong hires can see you burn through that without the results you’d hoped for. If you hire sales too early, you have an expensive AE with no real pipeline, no clear ICP, and no repeatable message. If you hire marketing too early, you generate interest without a defined sales motion to convert it. Once prospects turn away disappointed, it will be very difficult to win them back. The truth is, there isn’t a universal answer. It depends on your product, your pricing, and what the founder can already do themselves. In general though: Hire Sales first if: - You’re selling high-ticket, complex deals that require discovery and negotiation. - The founder is closing deals but running out of time. - You already have inbound or warm intros, but conversion is the bottleneck. Hire Marketing first if: - Your model relies on volume, lower annual contract value, or product-led growth. - The founders can sell, but nobody knows who you are yet. - You’re creating a new category and you need to create demand before outbound works. My advice to founders is to wait before hiring either role until you’ve personally closed your first 10 customers who didn’t already know you. Get it working yourself first. Then hire to scale it.

Jeremy Gnozzo at Search Solution Group said something this week that caught my attention: in 2026, precision will matter more than speed in hiring. And he’s right. A company rushes to fill a seat, then six months later everyone’s frustrated. What do we blame? We blame the speed of the hire. But speed isn’t the problem. Moving fast is fine when you know exactly what you’re looking for. The problem is ambiguity. Vague expectations. Undefined success metrics. Unclear authority. That’s what creates mismatched hires, not the clock. I've seen this everywhere from offices to film sets. So before your next hire, pause... Get brutally specific about what this role actually needs to deliver and how they’ll work within your system. The job description is the easy part. The real work is defining the role with enough precision that both you and your new hire know exactly what winning looks like. What’s one question you wish you’d answered before your last hire?

That realization made me think about something I often see in my professional life as well. For the past 2.5 years, I have been working in procurement consulting. One thing I have learned is that procurement is often an overlooked function in many organizations, even though it touches a large part of a company’s spending. Think about the number of things a company pays for every month, including internet services, cleaning and facility management, software subscriptions, security services, office supplies, consulting support, and many other vendor contracts. Individually, these costs might not seem significant. But when they run for years without being revisited, they slowly turn into background expenses — just like my phone bill! More often than not, the real opportunities are hidden within these overlooked areas, such as pricing structures, supplier fit, or the level of competition in the market. And that is why procurement (or, in other words, my job) really matters!

What is the downside of giving a state agency the authority to investigate and resolve those complaints? There is an obvious cost to run the state agency. Spread across millions of taxpayers, it is a relatively small cost per citizen. But many people don’t live in associations, and they have to subsidize the cost of resolving someone’s else’s grievance that has no impact on their life. But the question is more interesting when we look at the cost of running a state agency on a per-dispute basis. How much does it cost to resolve each dispute? According to the internet (so the data could be rough), our state received about 800 HOA complaints in 2018, when manager licensing was in effect. About 220 of those were manager licensing complaints. Some of these 800 complaints were duplicative, meaning that the same person filed the same complaint more than once. This is for a state that has about 2.5 million people living in HOAs. Also according to the internet, the office of HOA licensing operated on a budget of about $700,000 for 2018. So the cost to run the agency on a per-complaint basis in 2018 was about $3,200. That doesn't factor in the time of managers to respond to the complaints. I do know that in responding to some of the complaints, the time was significant. Others were disposed of without needing a response. Not all complaints are the same. Some involved serious violations that resulted in revocation of a license. Others were frivolous. The policy question in my mind is whether a complaining owner should pay a deposit or a fee for making a complaint with the state agency?

Sharing an observation that keeps confirming itself in real projects. I’m not claiming absolute truth, but there are clear signs that the traditional digital agency model may change significantly in the next few years. I’m talking about agencies whose business is built around a percentage of ad spend. This model has worked for the last 10–15 years, but today it’s becoming less stable. First, in-house teams are no longer expensive. The labor market has changed, and more companies prefer to build marketing internally. It gives better control, deeper product understanding, and direct connection to business KPIs (assuming KPIs are aligned across departments — which is another story). Second, technology is rapidly reducing the value of manual work. Campaign setup, optimization, and analytics are increasingly automated. The role of humans in classic media buying is gradually shrinking. Third, advertising platforms themselves are reducing the need for intermediaries. We see this across all global platforms: — stricter partner requirements — lower bonuses — smaller commissions, often moving toward zero The logic is simple: the more automation, the less the platform needs an agency. Fourth, agency economics are becoming fragile. Clients are used to paying a small percentage — sometimes 1–2% of the budget — and competition keeps margins low. In many cases, the model survives only because of platform commissions. Once those disappear, a large number of agencies will lose profitability. So the real question is not whether the market will change, but whether agencies will adapt in time. In my view, the window for strategic decisions is about one year. After that, the room for maneuver will shrink quickly. In two years, it may be gone. If you run an agency business, this might be the right moment to rethink the model. There are transformation scenarios available, but the time to think is getting shorter. Feel free to reach me out — let’s discuss. Every situation is different, but solutions still exist. For now, they still do.

Companies are just as confused about creating RFPs as they are about creating the software itself. And it makes complete sense when you think about it. The company is outsourcing a solution because they're not capable of building it themselves. That's great. But they're also the wrong people to write the RFP. Here's what actually happens: one person thinks of the solution they want, or three people try to write it simultaneously, or someone throws it through ChatGPT. The result is an RFP that prescribes solutions instead of describing problems. Then consulting agencies read that RFP and their goal is to win the contract. So they say yes to as much as possible, even if it doesn't make sense. They think they'll clear it up later during the SOW phase. But then what happens? The biz dev person at the agency and the main contact at the company want to get the contract done as fast as possible. The company wants to hit deadlines. The agency wants signatures so money can flow. Usually the biz dev people aren't the ones doing technical or design work. They're often paid on commission, which means they're super oriented to getting signatures. So if you try to slow down the SOW process to get clarity, it's not often successful. You launch a contract where the RFP was confusing, the SOW reflects that confusion, and now everybody expects the wrong things. The real solution? Companies should pay professionals to do a discovery process and write the RFP. People who understand technology, process, and design can write an RFP that enables agencies to show how they'll solve problems, not deliver to solutions that don't make sense. It's not even that expensive. But we've gotten away from this in tech. #ConsultingTruth #RFPProcess #DiscoveryMatters

I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

A hiring reality that often gets overlooked👇 The best engineers are rarely on the market for long. When a strong candidate starts exploring opportunities, things move quickly. Within a day or two they’re often already speaking with multiple companies and within a week or two multiple offers. But many hiring processes still move at a much slower pace. CVs sit in inboxes, feedback takes weeks, and interviews and decisions drag out over months. By the time a company decides they want to move forward… the candidate has often accepted something else. It’s not about rushing decisions. It’s about obtaining all the information required to make a decision in a timely fashion and recognising how competitive the engineering market is. If hiring is a priority, speed and communication make a huge difference: • Review profiles promptly • Share feedback quickly • Keep interview stages moving • Stay closely aligned with recruiters and candidates The companies that secure the best engineers usually aren’t the ones with the longest process. They’re the ones that move with intent.

You're not bad at making hard calls, you're just making them at the wrong time of day. In his latest piece, Phil McKinney challenges the old myth that decision-making “drains” like a battery. The research doesn’t support that story. What studies found instead is that after long periods of mental effort, your brain starts to change how it works. It leans toward what is faster and easier instead of what is deeper and more accurate. Careful thinking begins to feel like too much work, and your standards slowly drop without you realizing it. That is decision fatigue, and it usually shows up in small ways: - Nodding to a plan you would’ve challenged in the morning - Snapping at reasonable questions - Making a 30-minute decision in 30 seconds - Feeling relieved when someone else decides for you McKinney’s most practical advice is to stop relying on discipline in the moment and start building guardrails in advance. Pre-commitments such as setting rules about budget approvals late in the day, delaying responses to emotionally charged emails, or avoiding major hiring decisions at the end of the week create protection. They allow your high-energy self to safeguard your low-energy self. I featured Phil McKinney's insights in this week's issue of Exec Engineering. Recruiting Isn’t About Filling Roles — It’s About Solving Problems One of the biggest misconceptions about recruiting is that it’s simply matching résumés to job descriptions. It’s not. At its core, recruiting is problem-solving. When a company says: “We need a Senior Engineer.” What they often mean is: • We’re overloaded with projects. • Our junior staff need mentorship. • Clients expect more responsiveness. • We need someone who can own deliverables. • Leadership bandwidth is stretched thin. The job title is rarely the real issue. The operational gap is. The best hiring decisions happen when companies identify the actual problem they’re trying to solve — not just the position they’re trying to fill. On the candidate side, it’s similar. When someone says: “I need a new job.” What they often mean is: • I don’t see a growth path. • I’m underpaid relative to my value. • I’m not challenged technically. • Leadership isn’t aligned. • I feel stuck. Recruiting done well connects the underlying need — not just the surface-level request. That’s why alignment matters more than volume. You don’t need 50 applicants. You need the right solution. Reverse Recruiting in the UK! Is It even LEGAL? I’ve just read a recent piece discussing the rise of reverse recruitment. Where “career agents” charge candidates monthly fees and up to 10% of their salary to secure a role. This trend is growing fast in the US, and now appears to be creeping into the UK. But there’s a major problem:In the UK, it is illegal for recruiters to charge candidates to find them work. This isn’t a grey area. It’s clearly set out in UK law: The Employment Agencies Act 1973 prohibits agencies from charging individuals for finding them work (except in a few narrowly defined cases such as modelling and entertainment). The Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 reinforce this and regulate agency behaviour. GOV.UK also states plainly: “Recruitment agencies cannot charge you a fee for finding or trying to find you work.” Agencies can charge for optional services such as CV writing, training, or career coaching BUT they cannot make these a condition of finding you work. Some of these companies operate from the US or market themselves as “career agents,” not recruiters, positioning their fees as payment for coaching or networking support rather than job placement. But if a UK‑based business takes money in exchange for trying to secure you a job, it crosses a legal boundary. With unemployment rising and the job market tightening, the risk is that desperate candidates get exploited under the banner of “premium job‑search support.” My view UK jobseekers need to be very cautious. If you are paying anyone who claims to help you secure a role in the UK, ask direct questions: Are you compliant with UK recruitment legislation? Are you charging for coaching, or for job placement? Are your services optional or tied to finding me employment? Do you operate legally within the UK? If the answers get vague: Walk away! https://lnkd.in/ew-5kPzv

They hired their first recruiter from Google. Three months into Series A, hiring had stalled. She’d hired hundreds of engineers before. But this was a different game. At Google, engineers apply. Thousands of them. Your job is to filter. At a 30-person startup nobody has heard of, nobody is applying. Your job is to create demand. Two different muscles. Neither better. Just different. At Series A, you don’t need pedigree. You need someone who can build pull from zero. Someone comfortable reaching out cold. Someone who can make candidates reconsider their plans. If you’re hiring, get good at identifying future top 1% before the pedigree. The 4–5 year, battle-tested, “early OpenAI / Anthropic / Cursor engineer” profile is extremely hard to cold recruit. Not impossible but very hard for an early-stage startup. They’re saturated with inbound. They have liquidity (or a path to it). They operate inside dense, high-trust networks where the best opportunities circulate early (ex-Palantir, Stripe, and other “mafias”). By the time you reach out, they’ve likely already heard about the most compelling roles via text/coffee chats with friends, former colleagues, or investors. When they move, it’s usually via referral or a founder-level relationship. Elite recruiters do land these candidates but it takes a perfect storm. My cofounder Mike Cannon introduced a founder to an early Anduril engineer (first 20 hires) who was really considering the role. After that, the founder only wanted that level of pedigree. It’s not a scalable strategy for most startups, I’ve seen it and the results are roles that stay open for 6+ months. Bet on slope, not logo. Land the tenured Anthropic engineer before Anthropic. Build pattern recognition to spot great people early. If your strategy is to compete only for already validated pedigree, you’re competing at peak price and nowadays that’s north of $1M in total comp.

Agency does ~$500K in profit. Seller wants $1M cash at close. I hear this all the time. It’s a clean number. Feels like an exit. But the buyer math doesn’t care what feels clean. If a buyer has $1M of cash to deploy… they’re usually not buying a $2M agency. They’re buying a $4M–$5M agency. The math: At 25% down, $1M buys a $4M business. At 33% down, $1M buys a $3M business. Now translate that to profit: A $4M deal at 4x implies $1M of profit. So when a $500K profit agency asks for $1M cash at close? That ask eliminates most serious buyers. Sellers price from: “what I want.” Buyers price from: “what cash flow can support.” If you want more buyers, stop negotiating feelings. Negotiate reality.
Its crazy when you sit down and look at the numbers compared to just telling yourself youre good where youre at!

One of the most important things I learned from agency recruiting was to treat hiring like a sales pipeline. When you're working for commission, you learn that a part ofrecruiting is a numbers game. I needed to know exactly how many outreach messages it took to get a reply. How many screens to get a qualified candidate. How many final rounds to get an accepted offer. If I didn't track it, I didn't fill roles, which meant there wasn't money in the bank account Most founders, executive leaders, and hiring managers don't think this way. They post a job, interview whoever applies, and hope it works out. That's not a process, that's a prayer. Part of my role as a recruiting advisor is to educate. The hiring teams I work with now track their hiring funnel the same way they track their sales funnel. They know their screening-to-hire ratio. They know their average time to fill. They know their offer acceptance rate. And when something breaks, they know exactly where it broke. If you're hiring without metrics, you're flying blind. Your team is your most expensive investment, so act that way. P.S. - The focus on numbers and pipeline in this post is not at the expense of candidate experience and treating candidates as the people they are deserving of dignity and respect. #hiring #metrics #talentacquisition #startuphiring #recruiting #recruitingmetrics #startups

There's a number most lenders know but will never post about. It's the total amount they've spent on marketing that produced nothing. Not "underperformed." Not "could have been better." Nothing. For most lenders I talk to, that number is somewhere between $20,000 and $50,000. Exposed across agencies, lead vendors, consultants, and one very expensive "coaching program" they'd rather not discuss. One guy told me his number unprompted. $31,400. Two agencies. One lead vendor. Eight months total. The first agency charged $4,000/month. Delivered a beautiful landing page and a steady stream of leads. He funded one deal in four months. When he asked what went wrong, they said his "sales process needed work." The second agency charged $3,500/month. Promised they "specialized in lending." Turned out they also specialized in dental, HVAC, and personal injury. His ad account got flagged within six weeks for a compliance violation they didn't know existed. The lead vendor sold him 200 contacts over three months at $45 each. He called every single one. The conversations were brutal. Half had already talked to other lenders. A quarter didn't remember filling out a form. One guy asked him to stop calling and threatened to report his number. Total invested: $31,400. Deals funded from all three sources combined: 1. Commission on that deal: $9,500. He told me: "The worst part isn't the money. It's that I let it happen three times. After the first one failed, I should have known. But each one had a good pitch and I wanted to believe it would be different." I hear that sentence constantly. "I wanted to believe it would be different." That's not naivety. That's a lender who knows his business could be twice its size if someone solved the acquisition problem. Who keeps trying because the math should work — $10,000 commission per deal means you only need a few wins to justify the spend. The math does work. The vendors don't. Not because they're scammers. Most of them are competent at what they do. The problem is what they do isn't what you need. You need funded deals. They sell leads. You measure cost per funded deal. They report cost per click. You need someone who owns the outcome. They own the campaign and blame you for the rest. The $30,000 isn't a mistake you made. It's a gap in the market that nobody's filled — until you find someone who measures success the same way you do. If you know your number — the one you don't talk about — and you're done adding to it, DM me. I'll walk you through how we track cost per funded deal while giving you qualified closing appointments.

Companies are just as confused about creating RFPs as they are about creating the software itself. And it makes complete sense when you think about it. The company is outsourcing a solution because they're not capable of building it themselves. That's great. But they're also the wrong people to write the RFP. Here's what actually happens: one person thinks of the solution they want, or three people try to write it simultaneously, or someone throws it through ChatGPT. The result is an RFP that prescribes solutions instead of describing problems. Then consulting agencies read that RFP and their goal is to win the contract. So they say yes to as much as possible, even if it doesn't make sense. They think they'll clear it up later during the SOW phase. But then what happens? The biz dev person at the agency and the main contact at the company want to get the contract done as fast as possible. The company wants to hit deadlines. The agency wants signatures so money can flow. Usually the biz dev people aren't the ones doing technical or design work. They're often paid on commission, which means they're super oriented to getting signatures. So if you try to slow down the SOW process to get clarity, it's not often successful. You launch a contract where the RFP was confusing, the SOW reflects that confusion, and now everybody expects the wrong things. The real solution? Companies should pay professionals to do a discovery process and write the RFP. People who understand technology, process, and design can write an RFP that enables agencies to show how they'll solve problems, not deliver to solutions that don't make sense. It's not even that expensive. But we've gotten away from this in tech. #ConsultingTruth #RFPProcess #DiscoveryMatters

Common Fee Structures: Percentage of Salary: Standard 15-30% of the first-year compensation (base + bonus). Retained Search: Used for senior SAP leadership, involving an upfront fee (often 1/3 of total) and 25-35% total commission. I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

The person who figures things out under pressure is worth more than the one with the impressive title who needs everything defined. Desperation is the enemy of good hire. Hiring someone because you are overwhelmed and need a body in a seat is how you create a bigger problem six months from now. A bad hire at an early stage costs you time, culture, and sometimes key team members. Slow down to speed up. The right hire multiplies you. The wrong one drains you. You're not bad at making hard calls, you're just making them at the wrong time of day. In his latest piece, Phil McKinney challenges the old myth that decision-making “drains” like a battery. The research doesn’t support that story. What studies found instead is that after long periods of mental effort, your brain starts to change how it works. It leans toward what is faster and easier instead of what is deeper and more accurate. Careful thinking begins to feel like too much work, and your standards slowly drop without you realizing it. That is decision fatigue, and it usually shows up in small ways: - Nodding to a plan you would’ve challenged in the morning - Snapping at reasonable questions - Making a 30-minute decision in 30 seconds - Feeling relieved when someone else decides for you McKinney’s most practical advice is to stop relying on discipline in the moment and start building guardrails in advance. Pre-commitments such as setting rules about budget approvals late in the day, delaying responses to emotionally charged emails, or avoiding major hiring decisions at the end of the week create protection. They allow your high-energy self to safeguard your low-energy self. I featured Phil McKinney's insights in this week's issue of Exec Engineering.
