I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

Should you hire Sales or Marketing first? I’ve discussed with founders at early-stage startups and it’s something you really don’t want to get wrong. Startups have limited runway, and making the wrong hires can see you burn through that without the results you’d hoped for. If you hire sales too early, you have an expensive AE with no real pipeline, no clear ICP, and no repeatable message. If you hire marketing too early, you generate interest without a defined sales motion to convert it. Once prospects turn away disappointed, it will be very difficult to win them back. The truth is, there isn’t a universal answer. It depends on your product, your pricing, and what the founder can already do themselves. In general though: Hire Sales first if: - You’re selling high-ticket, complex deals that require discovery and negotiation. - The founder is closing deals but running out of time. - You already have inbound or warm intros, but conversion is the bottleneck. Hire Marketing first if: - Your model relies on volume, lower annual contract value, or product-led growth. - The founders can sell, but nobody knows who you are yet. - You’re creating a new category and you need to create demand before outbound works. My advice to founders is to wait before hiring either role until you’ve personally closed your first 10 customers who didn’t already know you. Get it working yourself first. Then hire to scale it.

Here's a frequent tension we see in the best / fastest growing Hard Tech startups: Demand for product is real. Customers want it yesterday. Need is urgent. BD team / leadership want to deliver on it and vacuum up all the demand today. This is the core of what drives fundraising momentum, especially at growth stages. But engineering needs to actually build the product(s)! And they're short resources. Hiring is hard. BD pushes forward anyway. "We won the contract!" Head of Engineering says "but how do we resource it / prioritize?" Engineering gets mad at BD for going too fast. BD gets mad at engineering for being negative. CEO is caught in the middle needing to pick a side. Investors want more revenue. Customers want things on time. Engineering wants to deliver great work ahead of schedule. This is hard! Do you compromise on eng talent quality and hire faster to meet contract deadlines? Do you say no to new contracts you'd easily win to make sure you deliver on contracts you already have? What's the solve? It's not an easy one! Solve 1: give your leaders more agency than it might seem their experience warrants. If they have good judgement, they'll figure it out. Solve 2: give these leaders cash to solve the problem...if you can raise it. Solve 3: delay deliverables if you have to. You're likely already 2x faster than a legacy player anyway. But be transparent with the customer as things develop. It builds trust. Saying "no" to real contracts now feels safe, but may be long term damaging. It's hard to mobilize customer interest, need to strike while the iron's hot and resource aggressively in other ways. Anyone have different views on this?

Most startups get their first people hire completely wrong. Not because they hire badly. Because they hire too late - and then too fast. The founding team holds everything together through sheer willpower until about 30 people. Then the cracks appear. Hiring slows down. Offers start to get rejected. Two senior people leave within the same quarter. So they panic and hire a Head of HR. But the problem was never HR. The problem was that nobody ever defined what good looked like for this specific business, at this specific stage, with this specific culture. An HR hire without that foundation doesn't fix the problem. They just inherit it. The companies that scale their people function without breaking do something different. They answer three questions before they make a single people hire: 💡 What does the business need from its people in the next 18 months - not today? 💡 What does our culture actually look like right now, versus what we say it looks like? 💡 What people infrastructure needs to exist before we can hire someone to run it? The answers are uncomfortable because they likely delay the immediate decisions you crave. But they're the difference between a people function that enables growth and one that slows it down.

Jeremy Gnozzo at Search Solution Group said something this week that caught my attention: in 2026, precision will matter more than speed in hiring. And he’s right. Most leaders think they’re being precise when they write detailed job descriptions. But that’s not where the real work happens. Real precision means answering the hard questions before you post the role: -- What’s the actual pace of work? Are we talking startup speed or enterprise methodical? -- Where does decision-making authority really sit? What can this person own vs. what needs approval? -- What does success look like in 90 days? In six months? Be specific. -- What are the unwritten rules of how work gets done here? Here’s the thing; we’ve all seen it. A company rushes to fill a seat, then six months later everyone’s frustrated. What do we blame? We blame the speed of the hire. But speed isn’t the problem. Moving fast is fine when you know exactly what you’re looking for. The problem is ambiguity. Vague expectations. Undefined success metrics. Unclear authority. That’s what creates mismatched hires, not the clock. I've seen this everywhere from offices to film sets. So before your next hire, pause... Get brutally specific about what this role actually needs to deliver and how they’ll work within your system. The job description is the easy part. The real work is defining the role with enough precision that both you and your new hire know exactly what winning looks like. What’s one question you wish you’d answered before your last hire?

Recruiting Isn’t About Filling Roles — It’s About Solving Problems One of the biggest misconceptions about recruiting is that it’s simply matching résumés to job descriptions. It’s not. The job title is rarely the real issue. The operational gap is. The best hiring decisions happen when companies identify the actual problem they’re trying to solve — not just the position they’re trying to fill. On the candidate side, it’s similar. When someone says: “I need a new job.” What they often mean is: • I don’t see a growth path. • I’m underpaid relative to my value. • I’m not challenged technically. • Leadership isn’t aligned. • I feel stuck. Recruiting done well connects the underlying need — not just the surface-level request. That’s why alignment matters more than volume. You don’t need 50 applicants. You need the right solution. Reverse Recruiting in the UK! Is It even LEGAL? I’ve just read a recent piece discussing the rise of reverse recruitment. Where “career agents” charge candidates monthly fees and up to 10% of their salary to secure a role. This trend is growing fast in the US, and now appears to be creeping into the UK. But there’s a major problem:In the UK, it is illegal for recruiters to charge candidates to find them work. This isn’t a grey area. It’s clearly set out in UK law: The Employment Agencies Act 1973 prohibits agencies from charging individuals for finding them work (except in a few narrowly defined cases such as modelling and entertainment). The Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 reinforce this and regulate agency behaviour. GOV.UK also states plainly: “Recruitment agencies cannot charge you a fee for finding or trying to find you work.” Agencies can charge for optional services such as CV writing, training, or career coaching BUT they cannot make these a condition of finding you work. Some of these companies operate from the US or market themselves as “career agents,” not recruiters, positioning their fees as payment for coaching or networking support rather than job placement. But if a UK‑based business takes money in exchange for trying to secure you a job, it crosses a legal boundary. With unemployment rising and the job market tightening, the risk is that desperate candidates get exploited under the banner of “premium job‑search support.” My view UK jobseekers need to be very cautious. If you are paying anyone who claims to help you secure a role in the UK, ask direct questions: Are you compliant with UK recruitment legislation? Are you charging for coaching, or for job placement? Are your services optional or tied to finding me employment? Do you operate legally within the UK? If the answers get vague: Walk away! https://lnkd.in/ew-5kPzv

Sometimes the signals start to show up early: • hiring faster than pipeline actually exists • activity metrics replacing real ICP clarity • spray-and-pray outbound tactics • daily activity tracking replacing strategy • narratives shifting when reality catches up to forecasts None of this is unusual in startup land ( I worked in 4) It’s all fun and games. Scaling a revenue engine is hard and the pressure after a big round is very real. But if you’re an SDR or early in your sales career, learning to spot these signals early is a valuable skill. Startups can accelerate your career faster and pay above market Just remember the same conditions that create rapid growth can also create rapid resets. Sometimes the best thing you can do is pay attention.

Most companies automatically choose a big recruitment agency over a solo recruiter. ✅ More consultants ✅ Bigger brand ✅ Fancy office ✅ Coffee machines with more buttons than a keyboard But here’s what no one likes saying out loud… A solo recruiter will often work harder on your role than an entire agency team. Why? Because when a big firm takes your role, the recruiter has to work twice as fast and juggle dozens of clients just to cover the 80% fee they lose to their employer. They might say they’re your trusted recruitment partner… But they’re saying the same thing to 30+ other clients. When a solo recruiter takes your role… 😀 Your role pays our bills 😀 Your role keeps our business open 😀 Your role keeps our dream alive So ask yourself this: Who is going to value your role more? And while we’re here, let’s kill another myth. There is no secret candidate database. Every recruiter is using the same tools: 🔎 LinkedIn 🔎 Job boards 🔎 Referrals 🔎 Internal databases The difference isn’t access. It’s hunger. When companies say they have “a bajillion candidates on their database”, it means nothing if they’re outdated, irrelevant, or in the wrong sector. Yet companies still default to the biggest agency in the room because it feels safer. Next time you need recruitment support, ask a different question. Not “How big is your database?” Ask “How quickly do you get people hired?” As a solo recruiter, my average time to offer is under 20 days. It doesn’t matter if my database has 10 candidates or 10 million. What matters is getting the right one. We all say we should support independent businesses. But apparently that rule doesn’t always apply to recruiters. Just my view 😀 #Recruitment #Hiring #SoloRecruiter #AgencyLife #AndrewsRecruitmentGroup

While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

Companies are just as confused about creating RFPs as they are about creating the software itself. And it makes complete sense when you think about it. The company is outsourcing a solution because they're not capable of building it themselves. That's great. But they're also the wrong people to write the RFP. Here's what actually happens: one person thinks of the solution they want, or three people try to write it simultaneously, or someone throws it through ChatGPT. The result is an RFP that prescribes solutions instead of describing problems. Then consulting agencies read that RFP and their goal is to win the contract. So they say yes to as much as possible, even if it doesn't make sense. They think they'll clear it up later during the SOW phase. But then what happens? The biz dev person at the agency and the main contact at the company want to get the contract done as fast as possible. The company wants to hit deadlines. The agency wants signatures so money can flow. Usually the biz dev people aren't the ones doing technical or design work. They're often paid on commission, which means they're super oriented to getting signatures. So if you try to slow down the SOW process to get clarity, it's not often successful. You launch a contract where the RFP was confusing, the SOW reflects that confusion, and now everybody expects the wrong things. The real solution? Companies should pay professionals to do a discovery process and write the RFP. People who understand technology, process, and design can write an RFP that enables agencies to show how they'll solve problems, not deliver to solutions that don't make sense. It's not even that expensive. But we've gotten away from this in tech. #ConsultingTruth #RFPProcess #DiscoveryMatters

Should you hire Sales or Marketing first? I’ve discussed with founders at early-stage startups and it’s something you really don’t want to get wrong. Startups have limited runway, and making the wrong hires can see you burn through that without the results you’d hoped for. If you hire sales too early, you have an expensive AE with no real pipeline, no clear ICP, and no repeatable message. If you hire marketing too early, you generate interest without a defined sales motion to convert it. Once prospects turn away disappointed, it will be very difficult to win them back. The truth is, there isn’t a universal answer. It depends on your product, your pricing, and what the founder can already do themselves. In general though: Hire Sales first if: - You’re selling high-ticket, complex deals that require discovery and negotiation. - The founder is closing deals but running out of time. - You already have inbound or warm intros, but conversion is the bottleneck. Hire Marketing first if: - Your model relies on volume, lower annual contract value, or product-led growth. - The founders can sell, but nobody knows who you are yet. - You’re creating a new category and you need to create demand before outbound works. My advice to founders is to wait before hiring either role until you’ve personally closed your first 10 customers who didn’t already know you. Get it working yourself first. Then hire to scale it.

Here's a frequent tension we see in the best / fastest growing Hard Tech startups: Demand for product is real. Customers want it yesterday. Need is urgent. Solve 2: give these leaders cash to solve the problem...if you can raise it. Solve 3: delay deliverables if you have to. You're likely already 2x faster than a legacy player anyway. But be transparent with the customer as things develop. It builds trust. Saying "no" to real contracts now feels safe, but may be long term damaging. It's hard to mobilize customer interest, need to strike while the iron's hot and resource aggressively in other ways. Anyone have different views on this?

Most startups get their first people hire completely wrong. Not because they hire badly. Because they hire too late - and then too fast. The founding team holds everything together through sheer willpower until about 30 people. Then the cracks appear. Hiring slows down. Offers start to get rejected. Two senior people leave within the same quarter. So they panic and hire a Head of HR. But the problem was never HR. The problem was that nobody ever defined what good looked like for this specific business, at this specific stage, with this specific culture. An HR hire without that foundation doesn't fix the problem. They just inherit it. The companies that scale their people function without breaking do something different. They answer three questions before they make a single people hire: 💡 What does the business need from its people in the next 18 months - not today? 💡 What does our culture actually look like right now, versus what we say it looks like? 💡 What people infrastructure needs to exist before we can hire someone to run it? The answers are uncomfortable because they likely delay the immediate decisions you crave. But they're the difference between a people function that enables growth and one that slows it down.

Recruiting Isn’t About Filling Roles — It’s About Solving Problems One of the biggest misconceptions about recruiting is that it’s simply matching résumés to job descriptions. It’s not. At its core, recruiting is problem-solving. When a company says: “We need a Senior Engineer.” What they often mean is: • We’re overloaded with projects. • Our junior staff need mentorship. • Clients expect more responsiveness. • We need someone who can own deliverables. • Leadership bandwidth is stretched thin. The job title is rarely the real issue. The operational gap is. The best hiring decisions happen when companies identify the actual problem they’re trying to solve — not just the position they’re trying to fill. On the candidate side, it’s similar. When someone says: “I need a new job.” What they often mean is: • I don’t see a growth path. • I’m underpaid relative to my value. • I’m not challenged technically. • Leadership isn’t aligned. • I feel stuck. Recruiting done well connects the underlying need — not just the surface-level request. That’s why alignment matters more than volume. You don’t need 50 applicants. You need the right solution. The strongest placements I’ve seen happen when both sides are honest about what they’re truly trying to fix. Curious — what’s the biggest hiring or retention challenge you’re seeing right now? I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

What is the downside of giving a state agency the authority to investigate and resolve those complaints? There is an obvious cost to run the state agency. Spread across millions of taxpayers, it is a relatively small cost per citizen. But many people don’t live in associations, and they have to subsidize the cost of resolving someone’s else’s grievance that has no impact on their life. But the question is more interesting when we look at the cost of running a state agency on a per-dispute basis. How much does it cost to resolve each dispute? According to the internet (so the data could be rough), our state received about 800 HOA complaints in 2018, when manager licensing was in effect. About 220 of those were manager licensing complaints. Some of these 800 complaints were duplicative, meaning that the same person filed the same complaint more than once. This is for a state that has about 2.5 million people living in HOAs. Also according to the internet, the office of HOA licensing operated on a budget of about $700,000 for 2018. So the cost to run the agency on a per-complaint basis in 2018 was about $3,200. That doesn't factor in the time of managers to respond to the complaints. I do know that in responding to some of the complaints, the time was significant. Others were disposed of without needing a response. Not all complaints are the same. Some involved serious violations that resulted in revocation of a license. Others were frivolous. The policy question in my mind is whether a complaining owner should pay a deposit or a fee for making a complaint with the state agency?

Sharing an observation that keeps confirming itself in real projects. I’m not claiming absolute truth, but there are clear signs that the traditional digital agency model may change significantly in the next few years. I’m talking about agencies whose business is built around a percentage of ad spend. This model has worked for the last 10–15 years, but today it’s becoming less stable. First, in-house teams are no longer expensive. The labor market has changed, and more companies prefer to build marketing internally. It gives better control, deeper product understanding, and direct connection to business KPIs (assuming KPIs are aligned across departments — which is another story). Second, technology is rapidly reducing the value of manual work. Campaign setup, optimization, and analytics are increasingly automated. The role of humans in classic media buying is gradually shrinking. Third, advertising platforms themselves are reducing the need for intermediaries. We see this across all global platforms: — stricter partner requirements — lower bonuses — smaller commissions, often moving toward zero The logic is simple: the more automation, the less the platform needs an agency. Fourth, agency economics are becoming fragile. Clients are used to paying a small percentage — sometimes 1–2% of the budget — and competition keeps margins low. In many cases, the model survives only because of platform commissions. Once those disappear, a large number of agencies will lose profitability. So the real question is not whether the market will change, but whether agencies will adapt in time. In my view, the window for strategic decisions is about one year. After that, the room for maneuver will shrink quickly. In two years, it may be gone. If you run an agency business, this might be the right moment to rethink the model. There are transformation scenarios available, but the time to think is getting shorter. Feel free to reach me out — let’s discuss. Every situation is different, but solutions still exist. Companies are just as confused about creating RFPs as they are about creating the software itself. And it makes complete sense when you think about it. The company is outsourcing a solution because they're not capable of building it themselves. That's great. But they're also the wrong people to write the RFP. Here's what actually happens: one person thinks of the solution they want, or three people try to write it simultaneously, or someone throws it through ChatGPT. The result is an RFP that prescribes solutions instead of describing problems. Then consulting agencies read that RFP and their goal is to win the contract. So they say yes to as much as possible, even if it doesn't make sense. They think they'll clear it up later during the SOW phase. But then what happens? The biz dev person at the agency and the main contact at the company want to get the contract done as fast as possible. The company wants to hit deadlines. The agency wants signatures so money can flow. Usually the biz dev people aren't the ones doing technical or design work. They're often paid on commission, which means they're super oriented to getting signatures. So if you try to slow down the SOW process to get clarity, it's not often successful. You launch a contract where the RFP was confusing, the SOW reflects that confusion, and now everybody expects the wrong things. The real solution? Companies should pay professionals to do a discovery process and write the RFP. People who understand technology, process, and design can write an RFP that enables agencies to show how they'll solve problems, not deliver to solutions that don't make sense. It's not even that expensive. But we've gotten away from this in tech. #ConsultingTruth #RFPProcess #DiscoveryMatters

Recruiting Isn’t About Filling Roles — It’s About Solving Problems One of the biggest misconceptions about recruiting is that it’s simply matching résumés to job descriptions. It’s not. At its core, recruiting is problem-solving. When a company says: “We need a Senior Engineer.” What they often mean is: • We’re overloaded with projects. • Our junior staff need mentorship. • Clients expect more responsiveness. • We need someone who can own deliverables. • Leadership bandwidth is stretched thin. The job title is rarely the real issue. The operational gap is. The best hiring decisions happen when companies identify the actual problem they’re trying to solve — not just the position they’re trying to fill. On the candidate side, it’s similar. When someone says: “I need a new job.” What they often mean is: • I don’t see a growth path. • I’m underpaid relative to my value. • I’m not challenged technically. • Leadership isn’t aligned. • I feel stuck. Recruiting done well connects the underlying need — not just the surface-level request. That’s why alignment matters more than volume. You don’t need 50 applicants. You need the right solution. The strongest placements I’ve seen happen when both sides are honest about what they’re truly trying to fix. Curious — what’s the biggest hiring or retention challenge you’re seeing right now? A WORD TO RECRUITERS AND THEIR JOB PLACEMENT AGENCIES Almost every month I see new ads on LinkedIn (and other sites) for new agencies offering job assistance. And every one of them wants members to pay a monthly fee for services that may or may not land them any jobs. There are hundreds of services like yours. What makes yours the right choice? Job seekers don’t need another subscription service to pay monthly. They need recruiters who understand how to match real talent with real hiring needs — not firms that scan resumes for keywords and push them through applicant systems for hundreds of dollars per month. That isn’t recruiting. That's automation. Real placement means understanding a candidate’s strengths and building relationships with companies that actually need the talent. In legitimate recruiting, the employer -- not the job seeker -- pays the fee. Employers either pay a placement fee or a percentage markup (often 10–20%) on a contractor’s hourly rate for a set period of time. Many professionals are no longer willing to pay $300–$500+ per month for vague promises with no guaranteed outcome. With scams increasing on LinkedIn and elsewhere, skepticism is common sense. What’s more, most experienced professionals don’t need resume rewrites or generic coaching. They need access to real hiring managers and real opportunities. If your firm truly operates differently, explain: • Who pays your fee? • How do you engage employers? • What measurable results do you deliver? Transparency builds trust. Anything else raises concerns.

I want to share something important for fellow job seekers. Recently, I applied for a “Travel Agent” position advertised on LinkedIn. After applying, I was invited to attend a webinar, where it was revealed that the opportunity required a subscription fee to get started. While entrepreneurship and independent contractor opportunities are valid business models, they are not the same as traditional employment. A job typically means: • You apply • You are interviewed • You are hired • You are paid for your work • You do not pay to begin working When a role requires an upfront fee or ongoing subscription, it is not employment — it is a business opportunity. There is nothing wrong with offering independent travel agent programs. However, transparency is critical. Job seekers — especially those actively seeking stable income — deserve to know upfront if: • A subscription fee is required • There is no guaranteed salary • The role is commission-based • It is an independent contractor model Advertising such roles strictly as “jobs” without clear disclosure can be misleading and discouraging to individuals who urgently need reliable income. Clear and honest communication builds trust. As professionals, we should ensure that opportunities are presented accurately so candidates can make informed decisions. I hope companies take this into consideration moving forward.

Should you hire Sales or Marketing first? I’ve discussed with founders at early-stage startups and it’s something you really don’t want to get wrong. Startups have limited runway, and making the wrong hires can see you burn through that without the results you’d hoped for. If you hire sales too early, you have an expensive AE with no real pipeline, no clear ICP, and no repeatable message. If you hire marketing too early, you generate interest without a defined sales motion to convert it. Once prospects turn away disappointed, it will be very difficult to win them back. The truth is, there isn’t a universal answer. It depends on your product, your pricing, and what the founder can already do themselves. In general though: Hire Sales first if: - You’re selling high-ticket, complex deals that require discovery and negotiation. - The founder is closing deals but running out of time. - You already have inbound or warm intros, but conversion is the bottleneck. Hire Marketing first if: - Your model relies on volume, lower annual contract value, or product-led growth. - The founders can sell, but nobody knows who you are yet. - You’re creating a new category and you need to create demand before outbound works. My advice to founders is to wait before hiring either role until you’ve personally closed your first 10 customers who didn’t already know you. Get it working yourself first. Then hire to scale it.

Startup Hiring 101 Your First 10 Hires Most startups don’t fail because of bad products, they fail because of bad hires. You need builders, not managers at first. Your first 10 hires set your culture permanently. Whether you are intentional about it or not, those first 10 people define how decisions get made, how conflict gets handled, and what “good” looks like inside your company. Choose deliberately. Skills you can train. Values you cannot. In early hiring, character and adaptability matter more than a perfect resume. The person who figures things out under pressure is worth more than the one with the impressive title who needs everything defined. Desperation is the enemy of good hire. Hiring someone because you are overwhelmed and need a body in a seat is how you create a bigger problem six months from now. A bad hire at an early stage costs you time, culture, and sometimes key team members. Slow down to speed up. The right hire multiplies you. The wrong one drains you. Here's a frequent tension we see in the best / fastest growing Hard Tech startups: Demand for product is real. Customers want it yesterday. Need is urgent. BD team / leadership want to deliver on it and vacuum up all the demand today. This is the core of what drives fundraising momentum, especially at growth stages. But engineering needs to actually build the product(s)! And they're short resources. Hiring is hard. BD pushes forward anyway. "We won the contract!" Head of Engineering says "but how do we resource it / prioritize?" Engineering gets mad at BD for going too fast. BD gets mad at engineering for being negative. CEO is caught in the middle needing to pick a side. Investors want more revenue. Customers want things on time. Engineering wants to deliver great work ahead of schedule. This is hard! Do you compromise on eng talent quality and hire faster to meet contract deadlines? Do you say no to new contracts you'd easily win to make sure you deliver on contracts you already have? What's the solve? It's not an easy one! Solve 1: give your leaders more agency than it might seem their experience warrants. If they have good judgement, they'll figure it out. Solve 2: give these leaders cash to solve the problem...if you can raise it. Solve 3: delay deliverables if you have to. You're likely already 2x faster than a legacy player anyway. But be transparent with the customer as things develop. It builds trust. Saying "no" to real contracts now feels safe, but may be long term damaging. It's hard to mobilize customer interest, need to strike while the iron's hot and resource aggressively in other ways. Anyone have different views on this?

Most startups get their first people hire completely wrong. Not because they hire badly. Because they hire too late - and then too fast. The founding team holds everything together through sheer willpower until about 30 people. Then the cracks appear. Hiring slows down. Offers start to get rejected. Two senior people leave within the same quarter. So they panic and hire a Head of HR. But the problem was never HR. The problem was that nobody ever defined what good looked like for this specific business, at this specific stage, with this specific culture. An HR hire without that foundation doesn't fix the problem. They just inherit it. The companies that scale their people function without breaking do something different. They answer three questions before they make a single people hire: 💡 What does the business need from its people in the next 18 months - not today? 💡 What does our culture actually look like right now, versus what we say it looks like? 💡 What people infrastructure needs to exist before we can hire someone to run it? What is the downside of giving a state agency the authority to investigate and resolve those complaints? There is an obvious cost to run the state agency. Spread across millions of taxpayers, it is a relatively small cost per citizen. But many people don’t live in associations, and they have to subsidize the cost of resolving someone’s else’s grievance that has no impact on their life. But the question is more interesting when we look at the cost of running a state agency on a per-dispute basis. How much does it cost to resolve each dispute? According to the internet (so the data could be rough), our state received about 800 HOA complaints in 2018, when manager licensing was in effect. About 220 of those were manager licensing complaints. Some of these 800 complaints were duplicative, meaning that the same person filed the same complaint more than once. This is for a state that has about 2.5 million people living in HOAs. Also according to the internet, the office of HOA licensing operated on a budget of about $700,000 for 2018. So the cost to run the agency on a per-complaint basis in 2018 was about $3,200. That doesn't factor in the time of managers to respond to the complaints. I do know that in responding to some of the complaints, the time was significant. Others were disposed of without needing a response. Not all complaints are the same. Some involved serious violations that resulted in revocation of a license. Others were frivolous. The policy question in my mind is whether a complaining owner should pay a deposit or a fee for making a complaint with the state agency?

Many individuals exploring new opportunities choose to work with recruiters, but doing so can sometimes limit your options. When a recruiter submits your resume to a firm on your behalf, the firm is typically required to pay a placement fee if you are hired. In many cases, that fee can be 20% or more of the starting salary. Because of this, some firms may choose not to pursue a candidate they otherwise might have considered if there were no associated recruiting fee. If there is a firm you are particularly interested in, consider reaching out to them directly. Sending a well-written, professional resume along with a thoughtful cover letter can significantly improve your chances of securing an initial conversation.
